topics.title: Upper and lower bounds in subtraction and division (applying bounds)

cards.front: The steps for the greatest possible value of a **quotient** such as speed $= \frac{d}{t}$.
cards.back: 1 Write the four bounds. 2 For the greatest quotient take the **largest numerator** and the **smallest denominator**. 3 Divide once, in one calculation. 4 Leave the full display. With $d = 150$ m (nearest 5 m) and $t = 12.4$ s (1 d.p.): $\frac{152.5}{12.35} = 12.3481781\ldots$ m/s.
cards.source: spec M4-NA-01; examiner report Summer 2023 M4 Q15

cards.front: $d = 150$ m to the nearest 5 m and $t = 12.4$ s to 1 d.p. Find the **least** possible speed.
cards.back: $\dfrac{147.5}{12.45} = 11.8473895\ldots$ m/s — smallest distance over longest time.

cards.front: $a = 8.6$ and $b = 3.2$, each to 1 d.p. Find the greatest and least possible values of $a - b$.
Trap: for the greatest value of $a - b$ you use both upper bounds, $8.65 - 3.25$. Why is 5.4 neither bound?
cards.back: Subtracting a bigger number makes the answer smaller, so the maximum needs the **upper** bound of $a$ with the **lower** bound of $b$. In a subtraction or a division the two bounds always come from opposite ends.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q17 (both upper bounds used in a subtraction)

cards.front: A lift holds 1500 kg to the nearest 100 kg. Each crate is 50 kg to the nearest 5 kg. Find the greatest number of crates it can certainly carry.
cards.back: $\dfrac{1550}{47.5} = 32.63\ldots$, so **32** crates — a maximum count is rounded **down**.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q13 (45 used instead of 47.5; some rounded up)

cards.front: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 9.4 m and one leg 6.2 m, each to 1 d.p. Find the greatest possible length of the other leg.
cards.back: $\sqrt{9.45^2 - 6.15^2} = \sqrt{51.48} = 7.17495\ldots$ m — the largest hypotenuse with the smallest leg, and no rounding until the end.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q17 (about 30% full marks)

cards.front: Trap: two heights are 172 cm and 165 cm, each to the nearest centimetre, and you give the greatest difference as 7 cm. What is it really?
cards.back: $172.5 - 164.5 = 8$ cm. The difference of the **rounded** values is never a bound; every bounds answer comes from substituting bounds.

cards.front: A calculation has two stages, for example a subtraction and then a division. How do you decide which bound to use at each stage?
cards.back: Work backwards from the target: ask at each operation whether a bigger input pushes the final answer up or down, and choose that bound. Substitute all the chosen bounds first, then calculate once.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q16 (bounds substituted into a formula)

cards.front: The four moves for any bounds question.
cards.back: 1 Write the half unit for each quantity (half of the rounding unit). 2 Write all the bounds. 3 Choose the bound of each input that pushes the answer the way you want, and substitute once. 4 Leave the full calculator display, unless an accuracy is stated.

cards.front: Greatest and least possible value of $a - b$?
cards.back: Greatest $= \text{UB}(a) - \text{LB}(b)$. Least $= \text{LB}(a) - \text{UB}(b)$.

cards.front: Greatest and least possible value of $a \div b$?
cards.back: Greatest $= \text{UB}(a) \div \text{LB}(b)$. Least $= \text{LB}(a) \div \text{UB}(b)$.

cards.front: A mass is $50$ kg to the nearest $5$ kg. What are its bounds, and why?
cards.back: $47.5$ kg and $52.5$ kg. The half unit is half of the rounding unit, and half of $5$ is $2.5$.

cards.front: Half unit for: nearest 2, nearest 0.5, 1 decimal place, 2 significant figures in 3400?
cards.back: $1$; $0.25$; $0.05$; $50$. Always half of the place the accuracy names — for significant figures, half of the place value of the last significant figure.

cards.front: A time is $1$ hour $11$ minutes to the nearest minute. How do you bound it for a speed in km/h?
cards.back: Change to minutes first: $71$ minutes, so the bounds are $70.5$ and $71.5$ minutes. Then divide by $60$: the shortest time is $70.5 \div 60 = 1.175$ h. Never write $1$ h $10.5$ min as $1.105$ h.

cards.front: Why can you not calculate first and bound the answer afterwards?
cards.back: Because squaring, dividing and square-rooting all change the size of a half unit. The bounds belong to the inputs, so substitute them and calculate once.

cards.front: A greatest possible number of whole items comes out as $28.46$. What goes on the answer line?
cards.back: $28$. A count of whole items is rounded down for a maximum, because the 29th item would not fit under any allowed load. A decimal on the answer line scores nothing.

cards.front: For $h = \dfrac{u^2}{2a}$, which bounds give the upper bound of $h$?
cards.back: Upper bound of $u$, squared, over twice the lower bound of $a$: $\dfrac{\text{UB}(u)^2}{2 \times \text{LB}(a)}$. $u$ is squared and $a$ is doubled.

cards.front: The bounds of a length are $6.0473\ldots$ m and $6.0518\ldots$ m. How do you state it to a suitable degree of accuracy?
cards.back: Round both bounds to $1$, then $2$, then $3$ significant figures and stop at the last accuracy where they agree. Both give $6.05$ to $3$ significant figures; at $4$ they give $6.047$ and $6.052$, so the answer is $6.05$ m.

cards.front: A display cuts off (truncates) at $1$ decimal place and shows $9.4$. What is the interval?
cards.back: $9.4 \le t < 9.5$. A truncated display is never above the true value, so the stated value is itself the lower bound.

cards.front: When may you round a bound?
cards.back: Only when the question states an accuracy. Otherwise leave the full calculator display: the CCEA schemes print values such as $53.19148936$ and $3.863512003$, and the accuracy mark follows the display.

topics.title: Factorising ax² + bx + c and more complex expressions (grouping, two variables)

cards.front: Before splitting any middle term, what do you always check for?
cards.back: A common factor of **all** the terms, numbers and letters together: $6x^2 + 9x - 6 = 3(2x^2 + 3x - 2)$. Taking it out first keeps the numbers small and is often worth a mark on its own.

cards.front: Show the grouping route for $6x^2 + 11x - 10$.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q20 (grouping problems)

cards.front: Factorise $2x^2 + 7x + 3$.
Factorise $3x^2 - 10x - 8$.
Factorise $8x^2 - 2x - 3$.
Factorise $4x^2 - 12x + 9$.
Factorise $2x^2 + 5xy + 3y^2$.
cards.back: $(2x + 3y)(x + y)$ — with two letters the same method works, and every term of the answer carries a letter.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2023 M4 Q19 (three-variable expression)

cards.front: Factorise $a^2x^2 - 4y^2$.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q18 (trouble with three letters)

cards.front: Factorise $\dfrac{x^2}{9} - 4y^2$.
cards.back: $\left(\dfrac{x}{3} + 2y\right)\left(\dfrac{x}{3} - 2y\right)$ — a fractional coefficient is still a square: $\frac{x^2}{9} = \left(\frac{x}{3}\right)^2$.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2023 M4 Q19 (most scored zero on the fractional case)

cards.front: Factorise $3 - 2x - x^2$.
cards.back: $(3 + x)(1 - x)$. When the $x^2$ term is negative, put the constants first in both brackets (or take out $-1$ and factorise $x^2 + 2x - 3$).

cards.front: Trap: you factorise $6x^2 + 9x - 6$ as $(6x - 3)(x + 2)$ and stop. What has been missed?
cards.back: The expansion is right but the factorisation is not complete: $(6x-3)$ still has a factor 3. Fully factorised it is $3(2x - 1)(x + 2)$.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q22 ("factorise fully")

cards.front: How do you check a pair of brackets when $a \neq 1$?
cards.back: Multiply the **outer** pair and the **inner** pair and add: they must give the middle term. For $(3x+2)(x-4)$: $-12x + 2x = -10x$. Also check the two end products give $ax^2$ and $c$.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q12(b) (wrong factorising gave the roots 40 and 6)

cards.front: For $ax^2 + bx + c$, the splitting pair multiplies to what?
cards.back: To $ac$, and it adds to $b$.

cards.front: What does 'fully' add to 'factorise'?
cards.back: Keep going until no bracket factorises, often a difference of two squares.

cards.front: State the difference of two squares.
cards.back: $a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)$, for any $a$ and $b$.

cards.front: $\frac{25}{49}x^2$ is the square of what?
cards.back: $\frac{5}{7}x$: square-root the top and the bottom.

cards.front: Grouping four terms: how do you choose the second factor's sign?
cards.back: Choose it so the second bracket matches the first.

cards.front: What comes out first from $6ax^2 + 9ax - 15a$?
cards.back: The common factor $3a$, numbers and letters together.

cards.front: $x^2 + 2xy - 8y^2$: what must each bracket keep?
cards.back: A $y$ beside each number: $(x + 4y)(x - 2y)$.

cards.front: How do you check a factorisation quickly?
cards.back: Expand the middle: the outer and inner products must add to b.

topics.title: Algebraic fractions with linear denominators: adding, subtracting and solving equations

cards.front: Write $\dfrac{2}{x+2} + \dfrac{3}{2x-1}$ as a single fraction.
cards.source: the spec's own worked example M4-NA-03

cards.front: Write $\dfrac{5}{x+1} - \dfrac{2}{x-3}$ as a single fraction.
cards.hint: Both terms of the second bracket change sign.

cards.front: Write $3 + \dfrac{2}{x-1}$ as a single fraction.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q18(b) (9% full marks with a whole number present)

cards.front: The common denominator of $\dfrac{2}{x+2}$ and $\dfrac{3}{2x-1}$ is ____.
cards.back: $(x+2)(2x-1)$ — the product of the two linear denominators, left in bracket form.

cards.front: Solve $\dfrac{2}{x+2} + \dfrac{3}{2x-1} = 1$.
cards.source: the spec's own worked example M4-NA-04

cards.front: Solve $\dfrac{4}{x} + 3 = 5$.
Solve $\dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{1}{x+1} = 1$, giving both roots to 2 d.p.
Trap: your equation has denominators $x + 2$ and $2x - 1$ and one root comes out as $x = -2$. What must you do?
cards.back: Reject it and say why: $x = -2$ makes a denominator zero, so the fraction is undefined. Check both roots against the denominators before writing them down.

cards.front: $\dfrac{a}{b} - \dfrac{c}{d} = $ ?
cards.back: $\dfrac{ad - bc}{bd}$

cards.front: Factorise $64 - k^2$.
cards.back: $(8 + k)(8 - k)$. Keep the order given: $(k + 8)(k - 8)$ is $k^2 - 64$, the negative.

cards.front: Which of these is printed on the Higher formula sheet: the quadratic formula, the difference of two squares, the rule for dividing fractions?
cards.back: Only the quadratic formula. a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) and invert-and-multiply must be known.

cards.front: A minus sign stands before a bracket. What happens to the signs inside it?
cards.back: Every sign inside the bracket changes, not only the first.

cards.front: How does a whole number $n$ join fractions over the denominator $D$?
cards.back: Write it as $\frac{nD}{D}$, then add its top to the other tops.

cards.front: Solve gives two roots and there is no context. Which go on the answer line?
cards.back: Both, unless one makes a denominator zero.

cards.front: What is the common denominator of two different linear brackets?
cards.back: Their product, left as brackets.

cards.front: In the quadratic formula $b=-9$. What is $b^2$?
cards.back: $(-9)^2=81$: bracket the $-9$ before squaring it.

topics.title: The quadratic formula and setting up/solving harder quadratic equations

cards.front: Solve $2x^2 - 7x - 3 = 0$ with the formula, to 2 d.p.
Solve $3x^2 + 5x - 1 = 0$ with the formula, to 2 d.p.
A right-angled triangle has perpendicular sides $x$ cm and $(x+4)$ cm and area 30 cm². Show that $x^2 + 4x - 60 = 0$ and find $x$.
cards.back: $\frac{1}{2}x(x+4) = 30 \Rightarrow x(x+4) = 60 \Rightarrow x^2 + 4x - 60 = 0$; $(x+10)(x-6) = 0$, so $x = 6$ ($-10$ rejected as a length).
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q15 (all or nothing on the "show that")

cards.front: A right-angled triangle has legs $x$ cm and $(x+7)$ cm and hypotenuse 13 cm. Form an equation and find $x$.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q12 (an area equation was written instead of Pythagoras)

cards.front: A rectangle $x$ cm by $(x+3)$ cm has a 2 cm by 2 cm square cut out of one corner. The remaining area is 50 cm². Find $x$.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q19 (an L-shape whose overlap was ignored)

cards.back: Multiply through by $-1$ first: $2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 0$, so $(2x+1)(x-3) = 0$ and $x = -0.5$ or $x = 3$.
cards.hint: Make the x² term positive before anything else.

cards.front: Trap: your value of $b^2 - 4ac$ comes out negative in an exam question. What should you check first?
cards.back: The signs of $a$, $b$ and $c$ after rearranging, and that $b$ was bracketed when squared. CCEA questions are set with real roots, so a negative discriminant nearly always means a sign or transcription slip.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q24 (negative b squared without brackets)

cards.front: How do you decide between factorising and the formula?
cards.back: Try the factors briefly: if the pair for $ac$ appears at once, factorise. If the question asks for decimals or a stated number of decimal places, the roots are not whole, so go straight to the formula on the sheet.

cards.front: Before you use the formula, what must one side of the equation be?
cards.back: Zero: rearrange to ax² + bx + c = 0 first.

cards.front: With b = −12, what is b² in the formula?
cards.back: 144: square the whole bracket, (−12)².

cards.front: What does (x + k)² expand to?
cards.back: x² + 2kx + k².

cards.front: In a show that from a triangle's area, what must the first line keep?
cards.back: The half: ½ × base × height.

cards.front: A root makes a side negative. What do you write?
cards.back: Reject it, with that reason.

cards.front: A diagonal is given. Which rule makes the equation?
cards.back: Pythagoras: the diagonal is the hypotenuse.

cards.front: When you split a compound shape into rectangles, what must not happen?
cards.back: Any region counted twice.

topics.title: Gradients of perpendicular lines and equations of perpendiculars

cards.front: The two lines drawn on the axes meet at right angles. Read each gradient from its equation and state the rule that connects them.
cards.back: One gradient is the **negative reciprocal** of the other: $m_2 = -\dfrac{1}{m_1}$, so $m_1 m_2 = -1$. Here $2 \times \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -1$. Not on the formula sheet.

image.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 200 200" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4"><path d="M20 100 H185" stroke-width="1.2"/><path d="M100 20 V180" stroke-width="1.2"/><path d="M73 154 L127 46" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 70 L160 130" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M106.3 87.5 L118.8 93.8 L112.5 106.3" stroke-width="1.2"/><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="10"><text x="130" y="44">y = 2x</text><text x="140" y="146">y = −½x</text><text x="188" y="104">x</text><text x="104" y="26">y</text></g></svg>
image.alt: A pair of coordinate axes with two straight lines crossing at the origin at right angles: one labelled y = 2x rising steeply, the other labelled y = minus a half x falling gently, with a right-angle marker between them.

cards.front: Give the perpendicular gradient for $m = 2$, for $m = -\frac{3}{4}$ and for $m = 1$.
cards.back: $-\frac{1}{2}$; $\frac{4}{3}$; $-1$. Turn the fraction upside down and change the sign.

cards.front: The steps for the equation of a line perpendicular to a given line and through a given point.
cards.back: 1 Rearrange the given line into $y = mx + c$ and read $m$. 2 Perpendicular gradient $= -\frac{1}{m}$. 3 Substitute that gradient and the given point into $y = mx + c$. 4 Solve for $c$ and write the full equation.
cards.source: examiner reports Summer 2024 M4 Q17, November 2024 M4 Q17

cards.front: Find the equation of the line perpendicular to $y = 3x - 5$ passing through $(6, 1)$.
Find the equation of the line perpendicular to $4x + 2y = 9$ passing through $(4, 7)$.
cards.back: $y = -2x + 4.5$, so $m = -2$ and the perpendicular gradient is $\frac{1}{2}$; $7 = \frac{1}{2}(4) + c$, so $c = 5$: $y = \frac{1}{2}x + 5$.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q17 (among the hardest questions)

cards.front: Trap: the given line is $4x + 2y = 9$ and you use $4$ as its gradient. What has to happen first?
cards.back: Rearrange to $y = mx + c$: $y = -2x + 4.5$, so $m = -2$. A gradient can only be read once $y$ stands alone with coefficient 1.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q17 (many scored zero for this reason)

cards.front: Trap: the question prints two coordinates as well as the line, and you work out a gradient from those two points. Why is that fatal?
cards.back: The gradient must come from the **given line**; the printed point is only there to find $c$. Examiners allow no follow-through from an invented gradient.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2023 M4 Q16 (a gradient of 7/6 invented from the coordinates)

cards.front: Trap: for a line of gradient 4 you offer a perpendicular gradient of $4$ or $\frac{1}{4}$. What is missing?
cards.back: The minus sign: it is $-\frac{1}{4}$. Reciprocal alone, or sign alone, is not enough — both changes are needed.

cards.front: Line $L$ is $y = 4x - 1$. Line $K$ is perpendicular to $L$ and passes through $(8, 5)$. Find the $x$ coordinate of the point on $K$ where $y = 23$.
cards.back: $K$: $m = -\frac{1}{4}$ and $5 = -2 + c$ gives $c = 7$, so $y = -\frac{1}{4}x + 7$. Then $23 = -\frac{1}{4}x + 7 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{4}x = -16 \Rightarrow x = -64$.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q18 (most found the gradient then stalled)

cards.front: What do you write the equation of a perpendicular line for, when the question does not ask for the equation itself?
cards.back: As a tool: once you have $y = mx + c$ for the perpendicular you can substitute a known $x$ or $y$ to find a missing coordinate, or test whether a point lies on it.

cards.front: One diagonal of a rhombus has gradient $\frac{3}{2}$. What is the gradient of the other, and why?
cards.back: $-\frac{2}{3}$: the diagonals of a rhombus (or a kite's axis and cross-diagonal) meet at right angles, so their gradients multiply to $-1$.

cards.front: Trap: what is perpendicular to the line $y = 4$, and why does the negative reciprocal rule fail here?
cards.back: A vertical line $x = k$. A horizontal line has gradient 0 and $-\frac{1}{0}$ is undefined, so this one pair is handled by the picture, not the formula.

cards.front: The diagonals of a rhombus have what special relationship?
cards.back: They bisect each other at right angles, so their gradients multiply to $-1$ and the crossing point lies on both.

cards.front: You have the equation of a perpendicular line and you are asked for a missing coordinate. What do you do?
cards.back: Substitute the coordinate you know into the equation and solve the resulting linear equation for the one you do not know.

cards.front: What must you do to ax + by = c before reading its gradient?
cards.back: Make y the subject, dividing every term.

cards.front: You have the perpendicular gradient and a point. What finds c?
cards.back: Put the point's coordinates into y = mx + c.

cards.front: A line through (0, k) has gradient m. What is its equation?
cards.back: y = mx + k: the point on the y-axis gives c.

cards.front: A line has gradient 3/8. What is the perpendicular gradient?
cards.back: −8/3: turn it over and change the sign.

cards.front: Perpendicular gradients multiply to give what?

topics.title: Frustums and compound solids: harder mensuration

cards.front: The dashed lines complete this solid into a cone. Name the solid, and write down how its volume is found.
cards.back: A cone (or pyramid) with the top cut off by a cut parallel to the base. Volume $=$ volume of the **full** cone $-$ volume of the **small** cone removed.

image.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 200 180" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><ellipse cx="100" cy="150" rx="55" ry="13"/><ellipse cx="100" cy="90" rx="30" ry="8"/><path d="M45 150 L70 90"/><path d="M155 150 L130 90"/><path d="M70 90 L100 18 L130 90" stroke-dasharray="4 3" stroke-width="1.2"/><g stroke-dasharray="3 2" stroke-width="1"><path d="M100 150 H155"/><path d="M100 90 H130"/><path d="M100 150 V90"/></g><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="10"><text x="126" y="146">R</text><text x="112" y="86">r</text><text x="104" y="124">h</text><text x="100" y="12" text-anchor="middle" font-size="8">apex of the full cone</text></g></svg>
image.alt: A frustum: a cone with the top removed, showing the base radius R, the top radius r, the height h of the frustum, and dashed lines continuing the sloping sides up to the apex of the full cone.

cards.front: The steps for the volume of a frustum.
cards.back: 1 Find the full cone's height, by similar triangles if it is not given. 2 Volume of the full cone $\frac{1}{3}\pi R^2 H$. 3 Volume of the small cone $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h_{\text{small}}$. 4 Subtract, keeping $\pi$ or the full display until the end.
cards.source: spec M4-GM-01; formula sheet gives the cone volume

cards.front: How do similar triangles give the height of the cone that was removed?
cards.back: The small cone is an enlargement of the full cone, so $\dfrac{r}{R} = \dfrac{h_{\text{small}}}{H}$. Halving the radius halves the height, so the cut at half the radius is at half the full height.

cards.front: A cone of radius 6 cm and height 12 cm has the top cut off halfway up, leaving a small cone of radius 3 cm and height 6 cm. Find the volume of the frustum, in terms of $\pi$ and to 1 d.p.
The steps for the total surface area of a compound solid.
cards.back: 1 List the faces that **touch the air**, naming each one. 2 Work out each area on its own labelled line. 3 Add. Hidden faces where two solids meet are never included.
cards.source: examiner report November 2024 M4 Q12 (examiners asked for each calculation to be named)

cards.front: A narrow cylinder stands on a wider one. What is the exposed area of the wider cylinder's **top**?
cards.back: A ring: the large circle minus the small circle, $\pi R^2 - \pi r^2$. The part covered by the narrow cylinder is not surface area.
cards.source: examiner reports November 2024 M4 Q12, M3 Q26

cards.front: A cylinder of radius 5 cm and height 4 cm has a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 5 cm standing centrally on top. Find the total surface area in terms of $\pi$ and to 1 d.p.
cards.back: Curved surfaces $2\pi(5)(4) = 40\pi$ and $2\pi(3)(5) = 30\pi$; base $25\pi$; small top $9\pi$; ring $25\pi - 9\pi = 16\pi$. Total $120\pi = 377.0$ cm².

cards.front: Trap: for two stacked cylinders you add the two complete surface areas. What does that count twice?
cards.back: The two circles where the cylinders meet — one is hidden entirely and the other is only a ring. Add faces, not whole solids.
cards.source: examiner report November 2024 M3 Q26 (many totalled both complete surface areas)

cards.front: A cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 10 cm has a hemisphere of radius 3 cm on top. Find its volume in terms of $\pi$ and to 1 d.p.
Trap: setting up a volume equation you write $\frac{1}{3}\pi 3r^2 h$ for a cone of radius $3r$. What is the correct term?
cards.back: $\frac{1}{3}\pi (3r)^2 h = 3\pi r^2 h$, because $(3r)^2 = 9r^2$. Bracket any scaled radius before squaring it.
cards.source: examiner report November 2024 M4 Q22 (3r squared without brackets)

cards.front: A cone of height 12 cm has volume $100\pi$ cm³. Find its radius.
cards.back: $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2(12) = 100\pi \Rightarrow 4r^2 = 100 \Rightarrow r^2 = 25 \Rightarrow r = 5$ cm.
cards.source: examiner report November 2024 M4 Q22 (radius of a cone from its volume)

cards.front: How is the **curved** surface area of a frustum built from the sheet formula $\pi r l$?
cards.back: Subtract the removed cone's curved surface from the full cone's: $\pi R L - \pi r l$, where $L$ and $l$ are the two slant heights. For the whole outside add the base circle and the top circle.
cards.source: packs/maths/exam-true/formula-sheets.json (curved surface area of cone is given)

cards.front: Trap: a compound-solid question asks for surface area and your working shows $\pi r^2 h$ terms. What is the quick self-check?
cards.back: Check the dimensions: every surface-area term has exactly two lengths multiplied ($\pi r^2$, $2\pi r h$, $\pi r l$), and every volume term has three. Label each line with the face it belongs to.
cards.source: examiner report November 2024 M3 Q26 (a large number calculated volumes instead)

cards.front: How do you find the volume of a frustum?
cards.back: Large cone minus small cone; each keeps its own radius and height.

cards.front: Cylinders of radii $R$ and $r$ are stacked. What area shows on the wider top?
cards.back: The ring $\pi R^2 - \pi r^2$: two circles subtracted.

cards.front: What is the volume of a hemisphere of radius $r$?
cards.back: $\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$, half the sphere's volume.

cards.front: What is the volume of a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$?
cards.back: $\pi r^2 h$; you must know it, as the sheet omits it.

cards.front: In a frustum question the radius is $3r$. What is $(3r)^2$?
cards.back: $9r^2$: the bracket squares the 3 as well.

cards.front: Which height goes in the cone's curved surface, $\pi r l$?
cards.back: The slant height l, never the perpendicular height.

cards.front: A division gives 7.8 containers. How many can be filled completely?
cards.back: 7: round down, since the eighth is not full.

cards.front: Two solids are glued together. Do the touching faces count in the surface area?
cards.back: No: they are sealed inside, so neither face counts.

topics.title: Circle theorems (use, with reasons; proofs excluded)

cards.front: $AB$ is a diameter of the circle, centre $O$, and $C$ is on the circumference. Find angle $ACB$ and give the reason.
cards.back: $90°$ — **the angle in a semicircle is a right angle**. It stays 90° wherever $C$ sits on the arc.

image.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 170 170" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="55"/><path d="M25 80 H135"/><path d="M25 80 L98.8 28.3 L135 80"/><path d="M106.8 39.8 A14 14 0 0 1 87.3 36.3" stroke-width="1.1"/><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="2.2" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="11"><text x="14" y="84">A</text><text x="140" y="84">B</text><text x="99" y="22">C</text><text x="72" y="94">O</text><text x="90" y="54">x</text></g></svg>
image.alt: A circle with centre O and a horizontal diameter AB. A point C on the upper circumference is joined to A and to B, and the angle at C is marked as the unknown x.

cards.front: $O$ is the centre and angle $AOB = 130°$. Find angle $ACB$ and give the reason.
cards.back: $65°$ — **the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference** when both stand on the same arc $AB$.

image.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 170 170" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="55"/><path d="M32.4 52.5 L80 80 L127.6 52.5"/><path d="M32.4 52.5 L80 135 L127.6 52.5"/><path d="M93.9 72 A16 16 0 0 0 66.1 72" stroke-width="1.1"/><path d="M88 121.1 A16 16 0 0 0 72 121.1" stroke-width="1.1"/><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="2.2" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="11"><text x="22" y="50">A</text><text x="132" y="50">B</text><text x="80" y="150" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="84" y="88">O</text><text x="80" y="66" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10">130°</text><text x="80" y="116" text-anchor="middle">x</text></g></svg>
image.alt: A circle with centre O. Radii OA and OB make an angle of 130 degrees at the centre, and the same chord AB is joined to a point C at the bottom of the circumference where the angle is marked x.

cards.front: $C$ and $D$ are both on the major arc $AB$, and angle $ACB = 40°$. Find angle $ADB$ and give the reason.
cards.back: $40°$ — **angles in the same segment are equal**. Both stand on the chord $AB$ from the same side of it.

image.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 170 170" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="55"/><path d="M28.3 98.8 H131.7" stroke-dasharray="4 3" stroke-width="1.1"/><path d="M28.3 98.8 L107.5 32.4 L131.7 98.8"/><path d="M28.3 98.8 L52.5 32.4 L131.7 98.8"/><path d="M112.3 45.5 A14 14 0 0 1 96.8 41.4" stroke-width="1.1"/><path d="M63.2 41.4 A14 14 0 0 1 47.7 45.5" stroke-width="1.1"/><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="11"><text x="16" y="104">A</text><text x="136" y="104">B</text><text x="110" y="26">C</text><text x="44" y="26">D</text><text x="104" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10">40°</text><text x="55" y="58">x</text></g></svg>
image.alt: A circle with a chord AB near the bottom. Two points C and D on the major arc above are each joined to A and B; the angle at C is 40 degrees and the angle at D is marked x.

cards.front: $ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral and angle $DAB = 105°$. Find angle $BCD$ and give the reason.
cards.back: $75°$ — **opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°**. The words "opposite" and "cyclic" both have to appear; "equal" is wrong.
cards.source: spec M4-GM-02; examiner report November 2025 M4 Q20(c)

image.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 170 170" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="55"/><path d="M32.4 52.5 L127.6 52.5 L122.1 115.4 L37.9 115.4 Z"/><path d="M47.4 52.5 A15 15 0 0 1 33.7 67.4" stroke-width="1.1"/><path d="M107.1 115.4 A15 15 0 0 1 123.4 100.5" stroke-width="1.1"/><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="11"><text x="22" y="50">A</text><text x="132" y="50">B</text><text x="126" y="126">C</text><text x="28" y="126">D</text><text x="46" y="72" font-size="10">105°</text><text x="108" y="106">x</text></g></svg>
image.alt: A circle with four points A, B, C and D on it joined in order to form a cyclic quadrilateral. The angle at A is 105 degrees and the opposite angle at C is marked x.

cards.front: $PT$ is a tangent touching the circle at $T$, and $O$ is the centre. Find angle $OTP$ and give the reason.
cards.back: $90°$ — **a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact**. This is one of only two guaranteed right angles in circle work.

image.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 170 170" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="55"/><path d="M15 135 H150" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M80 80 V135"/><path d="M94 135 A14 14 0 0 0 80 121" stroke-width="1.1"/><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="2.2" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="11"><text x="70" y="76">O</text><text x="72" y="150">T</text><text x="152" y="139">P</text><text x="87" y="131">x</text></g></svg>
image.alt: A circle with centre O and a tangent line touching the bottom of the circle at T. The radius OT is drawn and the angle between the radius and the tangent at T is marked x.

cards.front: $PA$ and $PB$ are tangents to the circle from $P$, and angle $APB = 44°$. Find angle $PAB$ and give the reasons.
cards.back: $68°$ — **two tangents from the same point outside a circle are equal**, so $PA = PB$ and triangle $APB$ is isosceles; the base angles are $(180 - 44) \div 2 = 68°$.
cards.source: examiner report November 2024 M4 Q15 ("isosceles" written without the tangent reason)

image.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 170 200" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="55"/><path d="M35.2 111.9 L80 175 L124.8 111.9"/><path d="M35.2 111.9 H124.8"/><g stroke-dasharray="4 3" stroke-width="1"><path d="M80 80 L35.2 111.9"/><path d="M80 80 L124.8 111.9"/></g><path d="M91.6 158.7 A20 20 0 0 0 68.4 158.7" stroke-width="1.1"/><path d="M50.2 111.9 A15 15 0 0 1 43.9 124.1" stroke-width="1.1"/><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="2.2" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="11"><text x="80" y="192" text-anchor="middle">P</text><text x="22" y="110">A</text><text x="130" y="110">B</text><text x="84" y="76">O</text><text x="80" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10">44°</text><text x="52" y="128">x</text></g></svg>
image.alt: A circle with two tangents drawn from an external point P below it, touching at A on the left and B on the right. The chord AB is drawn, the angle at P is 44 degrees and the angle PAB is marked x. The radii to A and B are dashed.

cards.front: The line through $T$ is a tangent, $TA$ is a chord, and the angle between them is $58°$. $C$ lies on the arc on the other side of $TA$. Find angle $TCA$ and give the reason.
cards.back: $58°$ — **the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment**. Cross the chord to find the segment the angle lives in.
cards.source: spec M4-GM-02; examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q19

image.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 170 170" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="55"/><path d="M15 135 H150" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M80 135 L135 80"/><path d="M135 80 L52.5 32.4 L80 135"/><path d="M94 135 A14 14 0 0 0 89.9 125.1" stroke-width="1.1"/><path d="M65.5 39.9 A15 15 0 0 1 56.4 46.9" stroke-width="1.1"/><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="11"><text x="70" y="150">T</text><text x="139" y="78">A</text><text x="42" y="28">C</text><text x="97" y="131" font-size="10">58°</text><text x="58" y="58">x</text></g></svg>
image.alt: A circle with a tangent touching at T at the bottom. The chord TA runs up to the right of the circle, and a point C on the far arc is joined to T and A. The angle between the tangent and the chord at T is 58 degrees and the angle at C is marked x.

cards.front: $O$ is the centre, $M$ lies on the chord $AB$ and $OM$ is perpendicular to $AB$. If $AB = 16$ cm, find $AM$ and give the reason.
cards.back: $8$ cm — **the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord**. With the radius as hypotenuse, Pythagoras then gives $OM$ or $OA$.

image.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 170 170" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="55"/><path d="M32.4 107.5 H127.6"/><path d="M80 80 V107.5"/><path d="M80 97.5 L90 97.5 L90 107.5" stroke-width="1.1"/><path d="M54.1 103.5 L58.3 111.5 M101.7 103.5 L105.9 111.5" stroke-width="1.2"/><circle cx="80" cy="80" r="2.2" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><g fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="11"><text x="22" y="112">A</text><text x="132" y="112">B</text><text x="74" y="122">M</text><text x="84" y="76">O</text></g></svg>
image.alt: A circle with centre O and a horizontal chord AB. A line from O meets the chord at right angles at M, and equal tick marks show that AM and MB are the same length.

cards.front: $OA$ and $OB$ are radii and angle $OAB = 34°$. Find angle $AOB$ and give the reasons.
cards.back: $112°$ — $OA = OB$ because **both are radii**, so triangle $OAB$ is isosceles and angle $OBA = 34°$; the angles in a triangle add to $180°$, so $180 - 68 = 112°$.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q17(b) (the hidden isosceles triangle)

cards.front: Which circle-theorem work is examined on this specification, and which is excluded?
cards.back: Using the theorems to find angles **with reasons** is examined. Their **proofs** are excluded by the Teacher Guidance, so no time need be spent learning to derive them.

cards.front: Trap: you write an angle of $76°$ with the reason "opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°", but the angle should have been $104°$. What do you score?
cards.back: Nothing for either part: a reason mark is tied to a correct angle. Work the angles out in order and check each against the diagram before writing the reason.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q20 (a wrong angle removed credit for its reason)

cards.front: On one arc, what is the centre angle in terms of the circumference angle?
cards.back: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.

cards.front: What do opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral do?
cards.back: They add up to 180°; equal only when both are 90°.

cards.front: What angle does a diameter make at the circumference?
cards.back: 90°: the angle in a semicircle is 90°.

cards.front: What angle do a tangent and the radius make at the point of contact?
cards.back: 90°: a tangent is perpendicular to the radius there.

cards.front: Two tangents from P: what goes before 'triangle PAB is isosceles'?
cards.back: PA = PB, because two tangents from the same point are equal.

cards.front: State the alternate segment theorem.
cards.back: The tangent-chord angle equals the angle in the alternate segment.

cards.front: Two points on one arc look at a chord. What is true of their angles?
cards.back: They are equal: angles in the same segment are equal.

cards.front: What is the first line of 'explain why this chord is not a diameter'?
cards.back: If it were a diameter, that angle would be 90°.

topics.title: Stratified sampling and estimating populations from samples

cards.front: What is a stratified sample?
cards.back: A sample in which every group (stratum) of the population contributes the **same fraction** of the sample as it forms of the population, so each group is represented in proportion to its size.

cards.front: The steps for working out a stratified sample.
cards.back: 1 Total the population. 2 For each group: $\dfrac{\text{group size}}{\text{population}} \times \text{sample size}$. 3 Round each to a whole number of people. 4 Check the rounded numbers add to the sample size, adjusting the one that was nearest to a half if they do not.

cards.front: A school has 720 pupils, 168 of them in Year 11. How many Year 11 pupils are in a stratified sample of 60?
cards.back: $\dfrac{168}{720} \times 60 = 14$ pupils.

cards.front: Three clubs have 142, 198 and 260 members. Work out a stratified sample of 45.
cards.back: $10.65 \to 11$, $14.85 \to 15$, $19.5 \to 19$: the three round to $11 + 15 + 19 = 45$, matching the sample size.
cards.hint: Round each, then check the total.

cards.front: Trap: a group's share works out as 10.65 and you write 10.65 on the answer line. What is wrong?
cards.back: A sample is made of whole people, so it must be a whole number. Leaving a decimal loses the final mark even when the calculation is right.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q15 (a decimal number of animals)

cards.front: A stratified sample takes 12 people from a group of 96, out of a population of 480. What was the total sample size?
cards.back: The group is $\frac{96}{480} = 0.2$ of the population, so $12 \div 0.2 = 60$ people in the sample.

cards.front: The steps for estimating a population by capture and recapture.
cards.back: 1 Mark and release a first sample. 2 Take a second sample and count how many are marked. 3 Set $\dfrac{\text{marked in second sample}}{\text{second sample size}} = \dfrac{\text{number marked altogether}}{\text{population}}$. 4 Solve, and give a whole number.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q15 (28% full marks)

cards.front: 60 fish are marked and released. A later sample of 80 fish contains 12 marked ones. Estimate the number of fish in the lake.
cards.back: $\dfrac{12}{80} = \dfrac{60}{N}$, so $N = \dfrac{60 \times 80}{12} = 400$ fish.

cards.front: Trap: asked to criticise a capture–recapture method you write "the sample was too small". Why does that rarely score?
cards.back: It is generic. Name a fault in the **described** procedure: the marked animals had no time to mix, some marks came off, animals moved in or out, or the second sample was taken from the same spot.

cards.front: Trap: a question asks whether a sample represents the population and gives you numbers such as "30% of 142". What earns the marks?
cards.back: Doing the calculation the data allows — $0.3 \times 142 = 42.6$ — and comparing the numbers. Listing memorised points about representativeness does not.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q18 (even able candidates overthought it)

cards.front: The group sizes have to be read off a histogram before the sampling can start. What comes first?
cards.back: Rebuild each frequency as **frequency density $\times$ class width**, total them for the population, and only then take each group's fraction of the sample.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q23 (most never got the frequencies right)

cards.front: Why is a stratified sample preferred to simply picking the first 60 people who reply?
cards.back: Volunteers are a biased sample: some groups are over-represented and conclusions drawn from them do not carry over to the population. Stratifying forces every group in, in proportion.

cards.front: In a stratified sample, what fraction of the sample comes from a group?
cards.back: Its fraction of the population.

cards.front: A stratified share works out at 9.6 people. What do you write?
cards.back: 10: round to a whole person.

cards.front: The sample comes from a subgroup only. Which total goes underneath?
cards.back: The subgroup's total, not the whole table's.

cards.front: In capture-recapture, which fraction matches the fraction of the population that is marked?
cards.back: The marked fraction of the second catch.

cards.front: Two catches of different sizes: is that a capture-recapture fault?
cards.back: No: the method compares fractions.

cards.front: Which word earns the mark for saying a stratified sample suits a survey?
cards.back: Representative.

cards.front: Marks wear off between the catches. Is the estimate too big or too small?
cards.back: Too big: fewer marked animals are recaught.

topics.title: Histograms with unequal class widths (frequency density) and estimating the median

cards.front: From the histogram, find the frequency of the class $20 < t \leqslant 40$.
cards.back: Frequency $=$ area of the bar $= 1.5 \times 20 = 30$.
cards.source: examiner report November 2025 M4 Q23 (area of a bar is its frequency)

image.alt: A histogram of time in minutes against frequency density with four bars of unequal width: 0 to 10 at density 0.8, 10 to 20 at density 2.0, 20 to 40 at density 1.5, and 40 to 70 at density 0.4.

cards.front: The steps for drawing a histogram from a table on a blank grid.
cards.back: 1 Add a frequency density column, $\text{frequency} \div \text{class width}$, for every class. 2 Choose a vertical scale that fits the largest density. 3 Label the axes "frequency density" and the measurement with its unit. 4 Draw each bar from boundary to boundary at its density, with no gaps.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q22(a) (many scored zero: own scales, unlabelled axes)

cards.front: Classes $5 < x \leqslant 15$ (frequency 24), $15 < x \leqslant 35$ (frequency 30) and $35 < x \leqslant 40$ (frequency 20). Find the three frequency densities.
Trap: you draw the bars at heights 24, 30 and 20 for those classes. What does the graph then show?
cards.back: Nothing usable — with unequal widths the **height must be the frequency density**, so those bars misrepresent every class. Bar heights equal to frequencies is the commonest zero on this question.

cards.front: What does "frequency density" mean in words, and what are its units?
cards.back: The frequency **per unit** of the measurement: how crowded the class is. For times in minutes it is people per minute, so a density of 1.5 means 1.5 people for every minute of that class.

cards.front: The four classes of the histogram have frequencies 8, 20, 30 and 12. Estimate the median.
cards.back: $n = 70$, so $\frac{n}{2} = 35$. Cumulative: 8, then 28, so the 35th value is in $20 < t \leqslant 40$, needing $35 - 28 = 7$ of that class's 30. Median $\approx 20 + \frac{7}{30} \times 20 = 24.7$ minutes.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2025 M4 Q22(b) ("continues to cause problems for the vast majority")

cards.front: Using the same histogram, estimate how many values lie between 20 and 30 minutes.
cards.back: Part of one bar: $1.5 \times 10 = 15$ values.
cards.source: examiner report Summer 2024 M4 Q21(b) (reverse reading was all or nothing)

cards.front: Trap: you give the median of a histogram as "$20 < t \leqslant 40$". Why is that only worth one mark?
cards.back: That names the class the median lies in; the mark scheme wants a **value** inside the class, found by going a proportional distance into it from the lower boundary.
cards.source: examiner reports Summer 2023 M4 Q21, Summer 2025 M4 Q22(b)

cards.front: frequency density = ?
cards.back: frequency ÷ class width

cards.front: The vertical axis of a histogram with unequal class widths must be labelled ____.
cards.back: Frequency density

cards.front: A population of N has g people in one group. How many of a stratified sample of n come from that group?
cards.back: g ÷ N × n, rounded to a whole number of people.

cards.front: Class 3.5 < x ≤ 5 has frequency 27. Frequency density?
On a histogram, what does the area of a bar show?
cards.back: The frequency of its class.

cards.front: Median inside its class: what fraction of the width do you move across?
cards.back: Values still needed ÷ the class frequency.

cards.front: An axis with no numbers: what fixes the scale?
cards.back: The one bar whose frequency you are told.

cards.front: Estimating a mean from a histogram: which value stands for each class?
cards.back: Its midpoint.
